newsitem.title: CHINA: Thousands demonstrate in China after bankruptcy.
newsitem.headline: Thousands demonstrate in China after bankruptcy.

text.p: Police in southwest China dispersed thousands of angry factory workers who staged noisy protests this month after their employers declared bankruptcy, officials said on Thursday.
A few of the ringleaders of the demonstration had been arrested, an official of the city government of Mianyang in southwestern Sichuan province said.

He dismissed a report by the New York-based Human Rights in China that 100,000 people had been involved in the protests in late June and early July and that paramilitary People's Armed Police used to break up the demonstrations had injured more than 100 people and detained about 80.
"Just one or two people who were pasting up 'big character posters' and stirring up the crowd were arrested," he said.
"The rest were dispersed and no workers were injured," he said.

Worker unrest is one of the greatest fears of China's Communist Party leadership, still haunted by the international outrage that followed the bloody army crackdown on student-led pro-democracy demonstrations centred on Beijing's Tiananmen Square in June 1989.
Officials reached by telephone at local factories said several thousand people had taken part in the protests on July 7, but said the city was now calm.
The demonstrators were mainly from three silk and textile plants that had gone bankrupt, officials said.

"Several big state-owned enterprises have declared bankruptcy and the workers and their family members launched the protests so that they can ensure a basic standard of living," the Mianyang city official said.
Human Rights in China said in a statement from New York that the government had imposed a curfew in the city before using the paramilitary to crush the demonstrations.
The town remained under tight police control with many of the detained workers still in custody, the human rights group said.
"They are asking for new jobs, but the government can only give jobs to some of them," the city official said. "We can only resolve such problems step by step in line with the bankruptcy law."

Sichuan dissident Li Bifeng, 33, a former tax officer in Mianyang, had written an open letter calling on international labour organisations to intercede on behalf of the workers, Human Rights in China said.

In his letter dated July 16 and made available by Human Rights in China, Li urged international labour organisations to press the Chinese government to respect its promise to the Chinese people to safeguard their right to subsistence.

He also urged the unconditional release of all workers detained in the protests, medical treatment for those injured and severe punishment for corrupt officials responsible for the collapse of the state industries.
Reports of increasing numbers of daring protests by disgruntled workers have surfaced in China in recent years as economic reforms have resulted in lay-offs from lumbering state factories.

China's leaders this year have placed reform of loss-making state enterprises at the top of their economic agenda, pushing through with bankruptcies that they had delayed for years for fear of social unrest.
